title: The magnitude and importance of the project's contribution to the expected scientific, societal and economic impacts
content:
## 2.3 The magnitude and importance of the project's contribution to the expected scientific, societal and economic impacts

### What magnitude means for a single-fellow action

FIELDWISE is a 30-month European Fellowship carried by one experienced researcher hosted at Eötvös Loránd University (ELTE), with MATE, MVCRI and AgroVIR as associated partners. Its contribution to impact is therefore stated at the scale a fellowship can credibly reach and no further: not a deployed commercial product, but a validated method, a set of reusable research assets, and an evidenced route to users — each of which is deliberately designed to matter beyond the immediate crop (processing tomato) and the immediate geography (Hungary and Bulgaria). The magnitude of the contribution is expressed here through two honest devices: reach and reusability (what the outputs let others do after the action), and quantified project evidence rather than advance promises (what the project will actually measure). This sub-section does not restate the career measures of sub-section 2.1 or the dissemination, exploitation and communication mechanisms of sub-section 2.2; it argues why the results make a difference, and how large that difference credibly is.

### Scientific impact: reframing how agricultural AI is judged, and building assets that outlast the action

The project's central scientific contribution is to provide a framework for agricultural AI evaluated according to temporal, geographic and operational transferability rather than only retrospective accuracy, and to establish a methodological bridge between high-information proximal hyperspectral observations and scalable Sentinel-based prediction (project impact IMP-SCI). The importance of this reaches well beyond FIELDWISE, because agricultural machine learning is predominantly evaluated through retrospective metrics such as R², RMSE and F1-score, which can produce optimistic performance estimates that are unsuitable for actual irrigation management. Reframing the evaluation question — from how accurately a model reproduces the past to whether its signal survives across seasons, across countries and into commercial fields, and whether it arrives early enough to change a decision — addresses a field-wide weakness rather than a project-specific one.

That scientific contribution is not left as an argument; it is embodied in concrete, reusable outputs that persist after the fellowship: the Hyperspectral-to-Sentinel transfer library (D2.2), which carries an explicit transferable or hyperspectral-only verdict for every candidate feature (KPI K2); the FIELDWISE predictive engine/model card (D3.2), released with a published model card (KPI K4); and the Adaptation protocol (D4.3), which states the minimum local-calibration volume needed to move the model to a new agro-environment (KPI K6). The Adaptation protocol is the mechanism that scales the scientific contribution past its immediate scope: because the cost of adapting the method to a new setting is stated rather than left implicit, the approach becomes portable to further crops and regions beyond processing tomato and beyond the Hungary-to-Bulgaria pair. In magnitude terms, the project therefore delivers not a single trained model but a documented, transferable method with a known adaptation cost — a contribution to increased R&I capacity, output and knowledge transfer among European research organisations, and, through the physiology-to-geoinformatics bridge, to the spread of interdisciplinary approaches in the European R&I culture.

### Societal, environmental and agricultural impact: a large problem where better timing matters

The societal importance of the work follows from the scale of the problem it addresses. Approximately 30% of EU territory is affected by seasonal water scarcity in an average year, while climate change is expected to intensify drought frequency and severity and to increase both the agricultural area requiring irrigation and irrigation demand in already irrigated areas. Water scarcity already translates into agricultural yield losses and higher water costs (project impact IMP-AGRI). Against a problem of that magnitude, even modest improvements in the timing and spatial prioritisation of irrigation carry substantial agronomic, economic and environmental relevance, and processing tomato — whose productivity depends strongly on the temporal interaction between water availability, atmospheric demand and developmental stage — is a demanding, high-value test case in which those improvements can be demonstrated.

The environmental contribution (IMP-ENV) is stated with deliberate discipline. FIELDWISE contributes to the EU-level opportunity for water savings in irrigated agriculture by improving irrigation timing and prioritisation, but the project does not claim in advance that it will achieve a particular percentage reduction; impact is to be quantified from project evidence. That evidence is generated by the Field Decision Value report (D5.3), which computes decision value for at least two competing models and reports warning lead time, false-action rate and missed-stress rate (KPI K8). This is what makes the magnitude claim credible rather than promotional: the size of the environmental and agricultural benefit is measured against what the models actually deliver in decision terms, not asserted as a headline number the fellowship cannot yet support.

### Economic and technological impact: from prototype to a validated demonstrator with a named route to scale

The economic and technological contribution is to advance the work from a desktop research prototype to a scientifically validated DrR web MVP (D5.1), delivered by month 24 and serving stress probability, uncertainty, spatial risk, irrigation priority and temporal evolution (KPI K7), and to subject that MVP to external, inter-sectoral scrutiny through the AgroVIR functional/technical evaluation (D5.4), which covers all nine assessment dimensions (KPI K9). This external evaluation is the source of the project's evidence about whether the resulting technology meets actual agricultural software requirements (IMP-TECH) — evidence that a single academic actor cannot generate alone, and which raises the importance of the contribution from a research artefact to a technology assessed under operational expectations.

The route by which this contribution can scale beyond the action is named rather than left open: the FMIS integration roadmap (D5.5), delivered in month 30, states the required interfaces and the post-fellowship steps needed to embed FIELDWISE outputs into farm management information systems (KPI K10), giving the project a research-to-operation delivery path with a named post-MSCA integration route (outcome OC5). The economic magnitude of that route is indicated by the reach of the channel it targets: AgroVIR operates a farm management information system in production use across more than 745,000 hectares in eight countries, including Hungary and Bulgaria — the potential integration surface into which the roadmap is written, even though deployment itself is explicitly not promised within the fellowship. At the European level (IMP-EU), the MATE-MVCRI architecture directly investigates whether agricultural AI developed in one European environment can be transferred to another, contributing to a wider European question — how locally developed agricultural intelligence can become reliably transferable rather than remaining confined to the field in which it was trained — that bears on the competitiveness and knowledge-transfer capacity of European research organisations and on the strength of international, inter-sectoral and interdisciplinary collaboration.

### Honest bounding, and why it strengthens the magnitude case

The magnitude of the contribution is bounded truthfully. The web MVP is the research-to-operation demonstrator, not the primary scientific objective, and full commercial integration is not promised within the fellowship; no advance numeric target is set for water saving. These limits are not concessions but the reason the impact case is believable: the project claims exactly what its outputs and KPIs can evidence — a transferability-first evaluation framework, three reusable and documented assets, a validated and externally assessed demonstrator, and a named integration route — and each impact route (scientific, environmental and agricultural, technological, and European) terminates in a named deliverable and a tracked KPI. An evaluator can therefore check the size of every claimed contribution against a concrete, measurable output, which is what distinguishes a genuine contribution to the expected scientific, societal and economic impacts from an aspirational one.
